en: Break long sentences into short meaning groups with a tiny pause between them. It sounds calm and clear.
Pause at the / marks.
Never pause in the middle of a thought group.
In a two-minute answer, plan where you breathe. Breathe at the end of a group, never in the middle of one.
One breath per group.
Drop your pitch slightly at the end of a completed group.
Direction-giving is much easier to follow when broken into small chunks with pauses.
Presentations sound much more confident when chunked clearly, giving the audience time to process.
Stories flow better and build suspense when chunked at natural narrative breaks.
For Part 2 or Part 3 answers, chunk each supporting reason separately so the examiner can follow your structure.
A short introductory phrase is usually its own chunk, set off with a small pause.
Recipe steps naturally break into chunks at each action — pause briefly between them.
Comparisons chunk around each side of the comparison, with a small pause before the contrast word.
Describing data chunks around each trend or figure, giving the listener time to picture it.
Reading a formal email or message aloud still needs natural chunking, not a flat word-by-word read.
A relative clause ('which...', 'who...') is usually its own chunk, set off by small pauses on both sides.
Safety instructions need very clear chunking so each instruction is unmistakable.
As a sentence grows longer, the number of chunks grows too — practise adding one chunk at a time.
Structured interview answers chunk around each part of the story: situation, action, result.
An extra comment inserted mid-sentence is its own chunk, set off clearly on both sides.
Each half of this structure is its own chunk, with a small pause right before 'but also'.
Product demos chunk around each feature being shown, pausing to let it land before moving on.
Rule explanations chunk around each individual rule so listeners can follow along.
Time clauses are usually their own chunk, whether they come at the start or end of the sentence.
A second buildup drill, starting more complex and adding even more chunks.
Cause-and-effect sentences chunk around the cause and the resulting effect separately.
When listing several pros and cons in one breath, each point gets its own small chunk.
Workplace announcements chunk clearly so nobody misses an important detail.
Delivering difficult news benefits from extra-clear chunking, giving the listener time to absorb each part.
A tribute speech chunks around each memory or quality being honoured, with a pause to let it land.
Describing an image chunks around each element you notice, moving from general to specific.
Historical explanations chunk around cause, event and consequence.
Plot summaries chunk around each major turning point in the story.
Negotiation chunks around your offer and your condition, giving weight to each part.
Describing symptoms chunks around each separate symptom so nothing gets missed.
Itineraries chunk around each day or destination.
Budget explanations chunk around each category of spending.
Comparing offers chunks around each job's pros, with a clear pause before the contrast.
Troubleshooting chunks around each thing you've already tried.
Dream narration chunks around each strange or memorable moment.
Discussing environmental topics chunks around the problem and its consequence, common in IELTS Part 3.
City descriptions chunk around each feature you mention.
Hobby explanations chunk around what you do, why you enjoy it, and how often.
Nostalgic storytelling chunks around each remembered detail, common in IELTS Part 2.
Policy explanations chunk around the rule and its exception or reasoning.
Study-strategy talk chunks around each technique being described.
Tech explanations chunk around each step or feature.
Sports recaps chunk around each key moment of the game.
Health advice chunks around each recommendation.
Weather-pattern discussion chunks around cause and typical result.
Support calls chunk around each troubleshooting step you ask the customer to try.
Even dense formal text needs clear chunking when read aloud, or it becomes impossible to follow.
Personal decision-making chunks around each factor being weighed, common in IELTS Part 3 discussion.
A closing set — mark where you'd pause before checking the suggested chunks.

When a word ends in a consonant and the next starts with a vowel, join them into one sound group.
Never stop between the words.
The consonant becomes the start of the next word.
Two vowels meeting need a small bridge: /w/, /j/ or /r/ appears naturally.
go on → go‿w‿on
I am → I‿y‿am
law and order → law‿r‿and order (British)
Intrusive /r/ is common in British English.
In fast speech some sounds simply drop out, especially /t/ and /d/ between consonants.
next day → nex' day
friendship → frien'ship
must be → mus' be
A sound can change to match the next one, so the mouth moves less.
ten bikes → tem bikes
did you → didjou
won't you → wonchou
Natural spoken English uses contractions almost everywhere. Full forms sound formal or emphatic.
I am → I'm
I will → I'll
do not → don't
would have → would've
Small grammar words lose their full vowel and become a schwa when they are not stressed.
to → /tə/
for → /fə/
and → /ən/
can → /kən/
of → /əv/
a → /ə/
the → /ðə/
Stressed 'can' /kæn/ means emphasis.
When one word ends and the next begins with the same consonant sound, don't say it twice — hold it once, a little longer.
In non-rhotic British English, a silent final 'r' becomes pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel.
Auxiliary verbs at the start of questions often reduce heavily in fast, casual speech.
Longer phrases link across every word boundary, not just the first pair — practise the whole chain.
'Going to' before a verb almost always links and reduces in natural speech.
Very common greeting phrases are almost always run together in natural speech.
The final 's' sound links smoothly into the next word's vowel, just like any other consonant.
Put it all together — link, reduce and contract naturally across a whole mini-paragraph.
Unstressed 'him', 'her' and 'his' often drop the /h/ sound completely and link to the word before.
Before certain consonants, /t/ is often replaced with a quick catch in the throat instead of a clear tongue-tap.
The /t/ becomes a glottal stop.
An -ing verb ending in a consonant sound links smoothly into a following vowel, just like any other word-final consonant.
Dates link and reduce heavily in natural speech — 'of' almost disappears.
Modal verbs followed by 'have' link and reduce so heavily that 'have' sounds like 'of' to many learners — that's just how it's linked, not actually spelled that way.
Common weather phrases link smoothly across word boundaries just like any other everyday speech.
Common office phone phrases link naturally across word boundaries — practise them as whole chunks.
A second full-paragraph challenge — link, reduce and contract across the whole thing.
'A lot of' is one of the most common linked phrases in English — practise it as a single unit.
Song lyrics are full of natural connected speech — great, memorable practice material.
'Because' commonly reduces to 'cause' or 'cuz' in relaxed conversation, and links straight into the next word.
Verb endings link into the next word exactly the same way noun endings do.
Real conversation links across every turn, not just within one speaker's sentence.
'Them' frequently reduces to 'em (dropping the 'th') and links straight onto the verb before it.
Numbers link into the noun that follows exactly like any consonant-to-vowel or consonant-to-consonant pair.
Common location phrases link fully across every word boundary — practise them as one chunk.
'There's' links tightly onto the word that follows, especially before 'a lot of'.
Negative contractions link straight into the next word just like any consonant ending.
'And' between number parts reduces to a quick /ən/ and links both sides together.
Excuse phrases are said fast and casually, with heavy linking and reduction.
These extremely common phrases reduce and link so much they barely resemble their spelling.
Live commentary links almost every word together at high speed — great advanced listening/speaking practice.
This whole obligation phrase links and reduces into a single fast chunk in natural speech.
Unstressed 'your' often reduces to a quick 'yer' sound and links onto the next word.
Very informal spoken only.
Everyday offer phrases link smoothly across the whole sentence.
'Used to' links tightly and reduces when telling stories about the past.
When a word ends and the next begins with a similar (not identical) sound, they still often blend rather than being said as two separate sounds.
Common service-industry phrases link naturally across the whole sentence.
One more full-paragraph challenge pulling together linking, elision, assimilation and weak forms all at once.
This common linking phrase runs together into one smooth unit.
'Except for' links tightly, with the final /t/ often barely released before 'for'.
Everyday planning phrases link and reduce heavily in relaxed conversation.
Dramatic narration still links every word together — the drama is in the pacing, not gaps between words.
'Gonna' links the same way regardless of which pronoun comes before it.
One last full-sentence challenge mixing linking, weak forms and reductions together.
One closing set combining consonant-vowel linking, elision and a weak form all in one line.

/v/ links into 'it'; 'to' reduces to /tə/.

Intrusive /w/ bridges /uː/ and /ɪ/.
Insert a subtle /w/ glide between vowels.
Natural /w/ glide connects 'you' and 'are'.
Subtle /w/ glide avoids an abrupt glottal stop.
Intrusive /j/ bridges the high front vowels.
Natural /j/ glide between /iː/ and /æ/.
Subtle /j/ glide prevents hiatus.

Twin consonant: hold the /n/ slightly longer without releasing twice.
Geminate /d/: stop the airflow once and release on 'day'.
Twin /k/: do not release the first /k/ before starting 'coffee'.
Twin /t/: one elongated closure, single release.
Twin /p/: hold the lips closed through both words.
Continuous /s/: elongate the friction seamlessly.
Twin /m/: hold the nasal murmur smoothly.
Single extended stop on the alveolar ridge.
Hold the closure on 'right' and release into 'turn'.
Twin /k/: hold velar closure without a separate burst.
Palatalization: /t/ + /j/ merges into /tʃ/.
Palatalization: /d/ + /j/ merges into /dʒ/.
/t/ + /j/ blends smoothly into /tʃ/.
/d/ + /j/ blends into /dʒ/.
/t/ + /j/ assimilation.
Rapid speech assimilation of /t/ and /j/.
/d/ + /j/ blends into /dʒ/ in conversational speech.
/s/ + /j/ assimilates to /ʃ/.
/s/ + /j/ becomes /ʃ/ in fast speech.
/t/ + /j/ palatalization across word boundary.
Elision: /t/ drops between consonants /s/ and /n/.
Elision: /t/ is omitted between /ks/ and /d/.
/t/ is elided before /tr/.
/t/ disappears between /s/ and /f/.
/d/ drops between nasal /n/ and dental /ð/.
/d/ drops between /n/ and /r/ in rapid speech.
/t/ is dropped between /f/ and /m/.

Comfortable conversational English is roughly 120–160 words a minute. Slower is fine; long silent gaps are what hurt.
Speak in chunks, not word by word.
Keep moving instead of restarting sentences.
A short natural filler buys thinking time. Silence and 'uhhh' do not.
Thinking time: well… / let me think… / actually…
Softening: I mean… / you know… / basically…
Linking: so / because of that / on top of that / that's why
Use one filler, not five. Repeating 'you know' every sentence lowers your score in speaking exams.
Fluent speakers correct themselves without stopping completely — a small phrase bridges the fix.
